title: 2 Clement
subtitle: an unnamed preacher reads his sermon after the Scripture: repent while there is time
lead: 2 Clement is not a letter and was not written by Clement. It is a sermon, read aloud in a church service by a preacher who never gives his name: 'after the God of truth, I am reading you an appeal to pay attention to what is written' (19:1). He speaks to 'brothers', and at the end to 'brothers and sisters', who had once bowed down to idols of stone, wood and metal (1:6). His aim, in Lake's words, is 'to inculcate a high Christology, a pure life, and a belief in the resurrection of the flesh'. Think of Christ as of God (1:1); confess him by what you do, not by calling him Lord (3-4); keep the seal of baptism pure (6-8); this flesh will be judged and will rise (9); repent while you are still on earth, like clay before it goes into the kiln (8; 13; 16-17).

The sermon quotes Isaiah in the Greek Bible and quotes the Lord about a dozen times, and several of those sayings are in no Gospel (4:5; 5:2-4; 12:2). It calls a Gospel saying 'Scripture' (2:4). It came to be called the second letter of Clement because it was copied after 1 Clement in the manuscripts. No church counts it as Scripture. Eusebius already said that the ancients made no use of it, and Lake holds it 'clear that it cannot have been written by the author of I. Clement'.
facts: No church. It is not among the New Testament books of the Council of Trent (Catholic), Article VI of the Church of England, the Westminster Confession (Reformed) or the Second London Baptist Confession. In the past it came near the edge of the canon: Codex Alexandrinus copied it with the Bible, and the Apostolic Canons list 'Two Epistles of Clemens' among the New Testament books, after Jude and before Acts (canon 85).

Unknown. The sermon names no author; the name of Clement comes from the manuscripts' title. Lightfoot thought the preacher a leader of the church speaking to his own congregation; Harnack thought him a layman (Lightfoot's report).

Uncertain. Lake: 'between 120 and 170 A.D. is the period chosen by the general opinion of the best critics, and within these limits ±150 A.D. is most usually accepted', except by those who follow Harnack (about 166-174). Lightfoot preferred 120-140.
No place is named. Lake gives three views: Rome (Harnack), Corinth (Lightfoot) or Alexandria (other scholars).
A sermon (homily), read aloud from a written text after the reading of Scripture in Christian worship (19:1). Lightfoot called it 'the first example of a Christian homily'.

Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s), which breaks off in 12:5; the Constantinople manuscript (C, written by Leo the Notary in 1056, found by Bryennios in 1875); and a Syriac version in one manuscript of 1169 at Cambridge (Lake).
authorship: It names no author, no city and no event. The preacher speaks of himself only as 'a sinner through and through' (18:2) and as 'the one who reads among you' (19:1).

Codex Alexandrinus counts it as Clement's in its table of contents, though the top of the sermon's first page, where a title would stand, may have been cut away (Lightfoot); C calls it 'Of Clement to the Corinthians', and the Syriac 'the Second Epistle' of 'the same' Clement. Lake prints the subscription 'Of Clement to the Corinthians, letter 2' at 20:5.

Eusebius: 'there is said to be a second epistle of Clement. But we do not know that this is recognized like the former, for we do not find that the ancients have made any use of it' (Church History 3.38.4). Jerome: it 'is rejected by earlier writers' (Lives of Illustrious Men 15). Lake: 'it cannot have been written by the author of I. Clement'. Lightfoot pointed to its Gentile outlook (1:6; 2:3), against 1 Clement's sense of being heir to Israel, and to its use of the Gospel of the Egyptians, which Clement of Alexandria, for one, set below the four Gospels.

Harnack and Lightfoot both explain it by Corinth: the sermon was kept in the church's archives beside 1 Clement and later copied with it, until both were taken for letters of Clement (Lake's report). Harnack thought it the letter of Soter of Rome; Lightfoot, a Corinthian homily.

audience.to: A Christian congregation gathered for worship, which heard the sermon read aloud after the Scripture reading (19:1): 'brothers' and, at the end, 'brothers and sisters' (19:1; 20:2), with 'young people' among them (19:1), led by elders who taught and warned them (17:3, 5). They were Gentile converts who had once 'bowed down to stones and wood, gold, silver and bronze' (1:6), baptized ('the seal', 7:6; 8:6), tired of waiting for promises 'heard long ago' (11:2), drawn to wealth and pleasure (5:6-7; 10:3), and troubled by teachers who said that 'this flesh is not judged and does not rise' (9:1; 10:5).
audience.why: To call them to repentance while there is time, by keeping their baptism and their bodies pure, confessing Christ by deeds, and holding to the hope of the resurrection of the flesh. Knowing that it is a sermon read in worship changes how it reads: its loose quotations, its repetition, its 'let us' and its sudden turns are a preacher's, not a theologian's, and its hearers are the people in front of him, not the church at large.
views: Harnack: the letter Soter, overseer of Rome about 166-174, sent to Corinth (Eusebius, Church History 4.23.11), for which he probably used an old homily; kept at Corinth with 1 Clement (Lake's report).
Lightfoot: a homily preached at Corinth, where the Isthmian games explain chapter 7, kept in the church's archives and copied after 1 Clement.

Other scholars, Lake reports, think it an Alexandrian homily, from its theology and its possible use of the Gospel of the Egyptians; this 'explains the contents of the book more naturally' but not why it was joined to 1 Clement.

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Reads the sermon as a historical source: who wrote it, where and when (Lake's three views: Harnack's Rome, Lightfoot's Corinth, an Alexandrian origin; Lake's 120-170, most often about 150), how it came to stand after 1 Clement in the manuscripts, and its text (A to 12:5, then C and the Syriac).

lenses.name: New Testament and the sayings of Jesus
lenses.desc: Follows the sermon's quotations: Gospel sayings in forms close to Matthew and Luke, sayings in no Gospel, 'another Scripture' (2:4), Paul, Hebrews and 1 Peter, and what they show about the writings a second-century church read aloud.

lenses.name: Preaching and practice
lenses.desc: Reads it as a sermon: read in worship after the Scripture (19:1), calling for repentance while there is time, the seal of baptism kept pure, self-control, almsgiving, mutual warning, and the elders' teaching.

sections.b: The Plain English Translation is made from Kirsopp Lake's Greek text (Loeb Classical Library, 1912). Where Lake's text departs from a manuscript, or a manuscript or editor reads differently in a way that changes the sense, a variant entry gives the readings, as Lake's and Lightfoot's footnotes report them. Quotations of the Bible use the site's own wording of the verse where the preacher's Greek matches it (Isaiah 54:1 in the words of Galatians 4:27; Luke 16:13; Hebrews 10:23; 1 Peter 4:8), and are translated as he gives them where he differs; the notes mark each one. 'Brothers' stays 'brothers' until 19:1, where the Greek says 'brothers and sisters'. Key terms follow the rest of the site: 'elders', 'self-control', 'repentance', 'the seal', 'resident aliens', 'Gehenna'.

Lake calls 2 Clement 'a letter only in form, and scarcely in that, for the writer distinctly states (cf. Cap. XIX) that he is reading aloud, and implies that he is doing so in a meeting for religious worship: it is thus clear that it is really more a sermon than a letter.' The ending, recovered in 1875, settled the question for Lightfoot: the preacher addresses 'brothers and sisters' (19:1; 20:2) and says he is reading 'after the God of truth', that is, after the Scripture. Lightfoot set the scene beside Justin Martyr's account of Sunday worship, where 'the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read', and then the leader teaches (First Apology 67). The sermon's style fits: it explains a text phrase by phrase (2:1-3; 12:2-5), repeats its key words (repent, keep, flesh, reward), and speaks always in the first person plural.

sections.h: Where it came from: three views
sections.b: Lake: 'there is no commonly accepted view as to the community to which it was sent. Three views may be mentioned.' (1) Rome. Harnack thought it the letter that Soter, overseer of Rome about 166-174, sent to Corinth (Eusebius, Church History 4.23.11), for which Soter probably used an old homily; it was kept at Corinth beside 1 Clement, and later both were taken for letters of Clement. (2) Corinth. Lightfoot thought it 'an ancient homily of some unknown person in the church at Corinth', laying stress on the imagery of the games (chapter 7) and the Isthmian games near Corinth; it too was kept in the Corinthian archives. Lightfoot objected to Harnack that the Roman letter Dionysius mentions was written in the name of the whole Roman church, 'whereas our author speaks in the singular throughout'. (3) Alexandria. Other scholars, 'regarding the external evidence as practically valueless', point to its theology and its possible use of the Gospel of the Egyptians; Lake says this view 'explains the contents of the book more naturally than do the views of Harnack and Lightfoot, but fails to show why it was ever connected with I. Clement.'

The sermon names no event, so it can be dated only by its ideas. Lake: 'This is a very insecure guide, but probably the half century between 120 and 170 A.D. is the period chosen by the general opinion of the best critics, and within these limits ±150 A.D. is most usually accepted, except by those who agree with Harnack to identify II. Clement with the letter of Soter to the Corinthians.' Lightfoot proposed 120-140: the preacher calls the Old Testament 'the Books' and the New Testament (or part of it) 'the apostles' (14:2), uses an apocryphal Gospel as authoritative, introduces a saying of Jesus with 'God says' (13:4), and opposes a Gnostic teaching 'still in an incipient form', with no sign of Valentinus or Marcion.

sections.h: The sayings of Jesus and the Gospel of the Egyptians
sections.b: The preacher quotes the Lord about a dozen times. Some sayings match a Gospel exactly (2:4 with Matthew 9:13; 6:1 with Luke 16:13; the second half of 8:5 with Luke 16:10); some are close but different (3:2; 4:2; 6:2; 9:11; 13:4); and some are in no Gospel (4:5; 5:2-4; the first half of 8:5; 12:2; 13:2b). Lake says the source of 4:5 and 5:2-4 'is unknown: it is often supposed to have been the Gospel of the Egyptians, but there is no clear evidence of this.' For 12:2 the evidence is stronger: Clement of Alexandria, answering Julius Cassianus, gives nearly the same saying and says, in his Greek as Lightfoot prints it, 'In the four Gospels handed down to us we do not have the saying, but in the one according to the Egyptians' (Stromata 3.13). Lightfoot believed the preacher used that Gospel 'as authoritative, and apparently as his chief evangelical narrative'. The preacher also quotes 'the prophetic word' of 1 Clement 23:3-4 (11:2-4) and twice speaks of Scripture or 'the gospel' for Jesus' words (2:4; 8:5).

sections.h: The manuscripts, and where A stops
sections.b: Lake: the sermon 'is found in the two Greek MSS. (AC) of I. Clement, and in the Syriac version (S), but it is not in the Latin or Coptic versions', and it is 'never quoted by Clement of Alexandria'. Codex Alexandrinus (A), a fifth-century Greek Bible now in the British Library, has it after 1 Clement but breaks off in 12:5 ('From this point A is wanting'); Fenlon's article on the codex says that 'probably two' leaves are lost at the end. The Constantinople manuscript (C), written by Leo the Notary in 1056 and found by Bryennios in 1875, has the whole sermon, together with 1 Clement, Barnabas and the Didache. The Syriac version survives in one manuscript, written in 1169 and now at Cambridge (Add. 1700); the translation itself, Lake thinks, is 'probably not early', perhaps of the eighth century. Lightfoot noted that the Syriac calls 1 Clement 'the Catholic Epistle of Clement' and gives the second the simpler title 'Of the same (Clement) the Second Epistle', which he took as a sign that in some older Greek copy 'the First Epistle stood alone'. So from 12:5 to the end the Greek rests on C alone, checked by the Syriac.

sections.h: Beside 1 Clement, and in the early lists
sections.b: The sermon's place beside 1 Clement gave it some of 1 Clement's standing. Lake says that 'at least as early as the fifth century, and probably earlier, it was in some circles closely associated with I. Clement', though not in the Coptic or Latin churches, and that the 'second epistle' Western writers mention is a different work, the letter of Clement to James. Fenlon writes that in Codex Alexandrinus the Clementine letters appear in the table of New Testament books, so that they 'seem to have been regarded by the scribe as part of the New Testament.' The Apostolic Canons, which Lightfoot would place perhaps in the sixth century, list 'Two Epistles of Clemens' among the New Testament books, after Jude and before Acts (canon 85). The Arabic catalogue of Abū al-Barakāt (died 1324) says Clement 'has two letters' that 'make up one book from the collection of books of the new law reckoned in the Church'. On the other side, Eusebius said the ancients made no use of it (3.38.4), Jerome that earlier writers rejected it (15), Photius, as Lightfoot quotes him, that it 'is rejected as spurious', and the Stichometry of Nicephorus, by Lightfoot's report, places both letters among the apocrypha.

Read it as what it is: what Lightfoot called 'the first example of a Christian homily', and a window into a second-century congregation at worship. Its strengths are its urgency, its plain moral demands and its hope for the body. Its weaknesses are a loose way with quotations and some teaching that goes beyond the Bible, such as ranking fasting above prayer (16:4). The canon section below sets out who has used it, why it was set aside, and how it measures against the 66 books.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the Scripture reading was from the end of Isaiah
spec.body: This is Claude's own suggestion. The preacher says he is reading 'after the God of truth' and urges his hearers 'to pay attention to what is written' (19:1). His Old Testament quotations cluster in the last chapters of Isaiah: 54:1 (explained phrase by phrase in 2:1-3), 52:5 (13:2), 58:9 (15:3), 66:18 and 66:24 (17:4-5, and 7:6), with Isaiah 34:4 behind 16:3. If the lesson read before the sermon came from Isaiah 52-66, the opening exposition of Isaiah 54:1 and the closing use of Isaiah 66 would frame the sermon around the text the congregation had just heard. Lightfoot said that 'we do not even know whether the lesson to which he here refers was taken from the Old or the New Testament', and the many sayings of Jesus could point to a Gospel reading instead, so this remains a guess.

canon.summary: 2 Clement is an anonymous Christian sermon of the second century, copied after 1 Clement and so named after Clement of Rome. No church counts it as Scripture today. In the past it stood at the edge of the canon: Codex Alexandrinus copied it with the Bible, and the Apostolic Canons list 'Two Epistles of Clemens' among the New Testament books, after Jude and before Acts (canon 85).
accepted_by: Not Scripture: the Council of Trent's list of the New Testament books (1546), which ends 'one of Jude the apostle, and the Apocalypse of John the apostle', does not include it.

The Apostolic Canons list 'Two Epistles of Clemens' among the New Testament books, after Jude and before Acts (canon 85), together with the eight books of the Constitutions. The Council in Trullo (692) ruled that the eighty-five canons 'should from this time forth remain firm and unshaken', but rejected 'the Constitutions of the Holy Apostles [written] by Clement', because 'through the agency of those who erred from the faith certain adulterous matter was introduced' (canon 2). It does not name the two letters. This page found no present-day Orthodox statement that names 2 Clement in or out of the New Testament.

Here the sources say Clement's two letters were counted with the New Testament. Abū al-Barakāt (died 1324) wrote that Clement 'has two letters, which the 318 appointed. They make up one book from the collection of books of the new law reckoned in the Church' (trans. McCollum), and Reid (1908) that 'the Coptic-Arabic Church include with the canonical Scriptures the Apostolic Constitutions and the Clementine Epistles.' Yet Lake notes that 2 Clement 'is not in the ... Coptic' version of 1 Clement. This page found no present-day Coptic statement on it.

Not Scripture. Article VI receives the New Testament books 'as they are commonly received'; 2 Clement is neither among them nor among the 'other Books' the Church reads 'for example of life and instruction of manners'.

Not Scripture. The Westminster Confession lists the 27 books of the New Testament, 'given by inspiration of God, to be the rule of faith and life' (1.2); 2 Clement is not among them. Its next section speaks of the Apocrypha of the Old Testament, not of early Christian writings like this one.
Not Scripture. The Second London Baptist Confession (1689) lists the same 27 New Testament books (1.2); 2 Clement is not among them.

provenance.b: A Greek sermon by an unnamed preacher to a Gentile congregation (1:6), read in worship after the Scripture (19:1). Lake dates it 'between 120 and 170 A.D.', most often about 150; its place is unknown (Rome, Corinth or Alexandria in the three views Lake gives).

Lake: 'It is clear from the MS. tradition that at least as early as the fifth century, and probably earlier, it was in some circles closely associated with I. Clement'. It was copied after 1 Clement in Codex Alexandrinus (400s) and the Constantinople manuscript (1056), and translated into Syriac with it. Eusebius knew of it by the early 300s ('there is said to be a second epistle of Clement', Church History 3.38.4). Lightfoot traced its later use to writers of the 400s-500s such as Timotheus of Alexandria and Severus of Antioch, and found the first quotation that names it the Second Epistle 'to the Corinthians' in Severus, about 520; it had been called an epistle 'from the first'.

Until 1875 only the part in Codex Alexandrinus, to 12:5, was known. Bryennios's discovery of the Constantinople manuscript, and then the Syriac, gave the ending, which showed that the work is a sermon (Lightfoot).

rejected_why.h: Not used by the early church
rejected_why.b: Eusebius set it apart from 1 Clement at once: 'we do not know that this is recognized like the former, for we do not find that the ancients have made any use of it' (Church History 3.38.4). Jerome sharpened the point: it 'is rejected by earlier writers' (Lives of Illustrious Men 15). Lightfoot added that Hegesippus, Dionysius of Corinth, Irenaeus and Clement of Alexandria give no sign of knowing it; Dionysius, writing to Rome about 170, speaks of reading 'the former epistle, which was written to us through Clement' (Eusebius 4.23.11), from which Lightfoot concluded that 'he seems to know of only one letter of Clement to the Corinthians.'

rejected_why.h: Not by Clement, nor by an apostle
rejected_why.b: The sermon claims no author, and the name it bears is the copyists'. For the churches that weighed books by their link to the apostles, a sermon of the second century by an unknown preacher had no claim to stand beside them. Lake judged that it 'cannot have been written by the author of I. Clement', and Photius, in Lightfoot's quotation, says that 'the so-called Second Epistle ... is rejected as spurious'.

The preacher quotes a saying that Clement of Alexandria, answering Julius Cassianus, placed in the Gospel of the Egyptians: 'In the four Gospels handed down to us we do not have the saying, but in the one according to the Egyptians' (Stromata 3.13, in the Greek Lightfoot prints). Lightfoot saw in this a gulf between the sermon and the writers of the late 100s, who held to the four Gospels alone.

cited_in.b: Both quote Isaiah 54:1 in the same Greek words; Paul reads it of 'the Jerusalem above', the preacher of 'our church'. 2 Clement is later than Galatians and may depend on it or on the Greek Isaiah directly.
The saying the preacher calls 'another Scripture' stands in Matthew 9:13 and Mark 2:17 in the same words; the direction is that the sermon quotes the Gospel tradition.
Reid named 2 Peter 3:16, which counts Paul's letters with 'the other Scriptures', and 2 Clement 2:4 as the first two places where 'Scripture' is used of New Testament writings.
'Love lays a cover over a great number of sins' is quoted word for word; the sermon uses 1 Peter, not the reverse.
'For the one who made the promise is trustworthy': the Greek is that of Hebrews 10:23.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to how a second-century congregation worshiped, preached and lived, 2 Clement is of high value: Lightfoot called it 'the first example of a Christian homily', it shows Scripture read before preaching, and it shows the sayings of Jesus, some in no Gospel, being quoted with authority. Its text rests on two Greek manuscripts and a Syriac version, with only one Greek manuscript for the last third. It makes few historical claims and none about its author. Measured against the 66 books it mostly agrees with them, goes beyond them in its teaching on almsgiving and its ranking of fasting above prayer, and uses one saying from a gospel outside the canon.

sections.h: 1. A witness to second-century worship: high
sections.b: The sermon was read 'after the God of truth' (19:1), so it shows a service in which Scripture was read and then explained, as Justin describes about the same time (First Apology 67). It shows a Gentile church with elders (17:3), a concern for those who drift (17:1-2), regular meetings (17:3), and a struggle against teachers who denied the resurrection of the flesh (9:1). Because it was preached, not written for a learned reader, it shows what ordinary believers were told.

Two Greek manuscripts, of the 400s (A) and of 1056 (C), and a Syriac version in a manuscript of 1169. A ends in 12:5, so for chapters 12-20 the Greek rests on C alone, checked by the Syriac. Lake's footnotes mark about fifteen places of doubt; one verse (10:3) may have lost a line, Lake's text follows a Syriac witness against the Greek manuscripts in a few places (1:2; 7:3; 9:5), and editors have proposed corrections elsewhere (Lightfoot at 6:6, 10:3 and 16:3; see the variants).

The sermon names no author, place or event, and so makes no false claim. The title 'of Clement to the Corinthians' is the copyists' claim, not the preacher's, Eusebius doubted the letter, Jerome reports that earlier writers rejected it, and Lake judges that it 'cannot have been written by the author of I. Clement'. Its few statements about its hearers (former idol worshipers, baptized, led by elders) are what a preacher says to people who know him.

• Matches: Christ the Judge of the living and the dead (1:1, as Acts 10:42); salvation as mercy to the perishing (1:7; 2:7, as Luke 19:10); confession by deeds (3-4, as Matthew 7:21 and James 2); the resurrection of the flesh and the body as God's temple (9:1-5, as 1 Corinthians 6:19 and 15); the church as Christ's body (14:2, as Ephesians 1:23); love covering sins (16:4, as 1 Peter 4:8).
  • Goes beyond: the church created 'before the sun and moon' (14:1); 'the spirit is Christ' (14:4), where the New Testament speaks more carefully of the Son and the Spirit; and the saying of 12:2 from the Gospel of the Egyptians, treated as a word of the Lord.
  • Sits uneasily: the ranking 'Fasting is better than prayer, but almsgiving is better than both' (16:4), which no book of the Bible gives, and the line 'almsgiving lightens the weight of sin', which stands close to Tobit 12:9 and Daniel 4:27. The site's cards at Proverbs 16:6 and Tobit 4 give the churches' readings.
  • In Claude's analysis the sermon nowhere plainly conflicts with the 66 books, but its teaching on works is less carefully balanced than Paul's.

how_to_read.b: Read it aloud, as it was meant to be heard. Its repetitions and its 'let us' are a preacher's. Ask what it asked of the people in the room.

When the preacher quotes the Lord or the prophets, look the verse up. The notes show where he matches the Gospels, where he differs, and where he quotes sayings no Gospel has. These are words from an early church, not new Scripture.

Its call to repent and to show faith by deeds is strong and biblical. Where it says more than the Bible, about almsgiving and fasting, read it beside the Bible's own teaching and the cards that set out how the churches understand it.
